question.text: This man served as president of Princeton from 1902 to 1910 before being elected U.S. president in 1912.
question.clue: An ultimatum authored by this president after the Arabic Pledge was broken prompted the issuance of the similar Sussex Pledge.

swap.leadin: This policy was enforced by the Volstead Act.
swap.text: Name this policy, which banned the sale or prodution of alcoholic beverages in the United States between 1920 and 1933.
swap.clue: Wayne Wheeler drafted a bill that would enforce this policy.

question.text: Washington was invited by this President, who took office after the death of William McKinley. In his military career, this man fought with the "Buffalo Soldiers" as leader of the Rough Riders.
question.clue: He negotiated the Treaty of Portsmouth that ended the Russo-Japanese War, and also names a corollary to the Monroe Doctrine.

swap.text: The bloodiest battle of the war took place on this Cuban hill, which was near Teddy Roosevelt's Rough Riders and the Buffalo Soldiers on Kettle Hill.
swap.clue: Samuel Sumner commanded the cavalry since "Fighting Joe" Wheeler was deathly ill, but Wheeler rose from his sickbed to meet up with Jacob Kent, who had been dispatched by William Rufus Shafter.

question.text: This political party nominated Henry Wallace and Robert LaFollete as its candidates for President.
question.clue: Perhaps the greatest electoral successes of a party by this name came earlier, in California, where Hiram Johnson was elected governor and then Senator on its banner.

swap.leadin: The Dujiangyan ("DU-jiang-yan") is an engineering marvel, consisting of the Yuzui to divide water, Feisha Yan ("FAY-sha yen") to divert sediment, and Baoping Kou ("BAU-ping koh") to control the flow ratio between the two channels.
swap.text: The Dujiangyan is the oldest and only remaining dam-free irrigation system in the world, and is instead made of artificial channels for water to flow through. Artificial water channels are known by this term.
swap.clue: Yellow fever afflicted workers who built one of these structures across the Isthmus of Darien.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the history of conservation in the United States.
question.text: This man served as the first head of the U.S. Forest Service before he was fired after coming into conflict with William Taft's Interior Secretary, Richard Ballinger.
question.clue: This man's open letter to Senator Jonathan Dolliver of Iowa led to the climax of a scandal he was involved in, which began when Morgan and Guggenheim's "Alaska Syndicate" was accused of corruption by Louis Glavis.

swap.leadin: This man created the NNBL to promote African-American businesses and hired George Washington Carver to an institution where he popularized crop rotation.
swap.text: Name this president of Tuskegee University who asked African-Americans to "cast down your bucket" in his Atlanta Compromise speech.
swap.clue: Deborah Davis's Guest of Honor examines this man's dinner with Teddy Roosevelt as the first African-American to dine in the White House.

question.leadin: BONUS. Name these labor cases brought before the Supreme Court.
question.text: Justice Peckham wrote that a state law limiting the workweek of bakers violated the freedom of contract in this 1905 case.
question.clue: This case's decision lost influence with the "switch in time that saved nine" which ruled the government could restrict the liberty of contract in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish.

swap.leadin: Name these "amendments" governing the Latin American policy of the U.S.
swap.text: This law, named for the Connecticut senator who put it forth on behalf of Secretary of State Root, permitted an exclusive U.S. right to intervene in Cuba.
swap.clue: This legislation prohibited a certain entity from entering into debt that it could not pay, or from making territorial concessions to anybody except the United States.

question.text: Before he was a senator, Wagner chaired New York's investigation of this clothes company. A 1911 fire in this company's Manhattan factory killed 146 of its mostly female garment workers.
question.clue: Under Russian immigrant owners Isaac Harris and Max Blanck, this company moved to a high-tech loft space in the Asch Building.

swap.leadin: McClure's Magazine patronized many of the writers described by this epithet.
swap.text: Teddy Roosevelt provided what term for journalists who exposed the predations of large corporations around the turn of the 20th century?
swap.clue: This term was used to describe Henry Demarest Lloyd, the author of Wealth Against Commowealth, which critiqued an organization that was also exposed by Ida Tarbell.

question.text: After being reelected to the House of Representatives, Victor Berger was denied his seat when he was convicted under this act. The phrase "clear and present danger" originated in a case regarding this act.
question.clue: This 1917 legislation that Daniel Ellsberg was accused of violating for stealing and leaking the Pentagon Papers.

swap.leadin: Several of these cases arose from disputes over applying customs duties and tariffs to goods at the Port of New York.
swap.text: Name this series of 1901 Supreme Court cases, which metaphorically answered whether the Constitution follows the flag, finding the Constitution does not necessarily apply to territories.
swap.clue: This 1901 set of Supreme Court cases. These cases prevented newly-acquired U.S. territories from being incorporated into the Union based on the difficulty of enacting "Anglo-Saxon principles."

question.leadin: In an essay on the failure of this cause, Francis Parkman argued it was a "public pest" that destroyed the US.
question.text: Name this cause. The Nineteenth Amendment was the culmination of fights for this cause by women.
question.answerHtml: universal suffrage [or women’s suffrage; or the right to vote]
question.clue: A group of supporters of this cause had a convention in Akron, Ohio, during which Sojourner Truth gave a notable speech.

swap.text: This congressman used the data of the 1890 census to set the quotas for new immigrants in the Immigrant Act of 1924, which he co-sponsored and names with Senator David Reed.
swap.clue: This native Kentuckian served as aide-de-camp to Sam Houston during the war of independence, and then was named Texas's Secretary of War by Mirabeau Lamar. The leader of Confederate forces in the West, he was killed at the battle of Shiloh.

question.leadin: Answer stuff about Muckraking classics of the Progressive Era.
question.text: In this first collection of McClure's magazine articles published by Lincoln Steffens in 1904, he looks at the sources of urban political corruption, writing that the "big business man" is a "self-righteous fraud" who should keep away from politics.

swap.leadin: Name these things about the Panic of 1907.
swap.text: The next element of the panic was a run on this trust company after it fired its president, Charles Barney. It shares its name with the fictional persona Diedrich, which Washington Irving used to write A History of New York.

question.leadin: Name these things about the policy of "dollar diplomacy," FTP each.
question.text: The policy's strongest practitioner was this man, who resigned as a senator from Pennsylvania in 1909 to become William Howard Taft's secretary of state.
question.clue: When William Howard Taft tried to appoint this man Secretary of State, he was briefly considered ineligible because he had served in Congress when it voted a pay raise for the position. He was confirmed after the first "Saxbe fix" temporarily lowered his salary to the pre-raise level.

swap.leadin: She was the first president of the Negro Fellowship League, which provided assistance to black migrants in the north, and her life's work was chronicled in A Red Record and Crusade for Justice.
